overview: The Achaemenid Empire was the largest the ancient world had yet seen, stretching from the Balkans to the Indus Valley. Founded by Cyrus the Great, it pioneered tolerant multi-ethnic governance, monumental architecture and efficient long-distance administration.

items.text: The Royal Road stretched 2,700 kilometers from Susa to Sardis, with relay stations enabling messages to travel in nine days.
Qanat irrigation tunnels brought water from mountains to arid plains across Iran.
Standardized gold daric and silver siglos coins facilitated trade across the empire.
Persepolis built as a ceremonial capital with colossal stone columns, bull capitals and relief sculptures of subject nations.
The Cyrus Cylinder, sometimes called the first charter of human rights, records religious tolerance and the freeing of enslaved peoples.
Zoroastrianism practiced by the royal family, emphasizing cosmic struggle between truth and falsehood.
Cyrus permitted conquered peoples to keep their religions, as recorded in the Hebrew Bible for the Jewish return from exile.
The satrapy system divided the empire into provinces governed by appointed officials with local autonomy.
The empire connected Mediterranean, Central Asian, Indian and Arabian trade networks.
Aramaic used as the administrative lingua franca across dozens of languages and peoples.
The model of a tolerant multi-ethnic empire influenced all subsequent Iranian states.
Administrative practices adopted by Alexander, the Seleucids and later empires.
Persepolis remains Iran's most powerful symbol of pre-Islamic civilization.

fall.text: Alexander the Great defeated Darius III at Gaugamela in 331 BCE and burned Persepolis the following year.
